stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death of Evita
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of July, at eight twenty-five in the evening, Eva dies in the presidential residence, thirty-three years old, worn to nothing by the cancer. The radio breaks the news to a stunned country: the Spiritual Leader of the Nation has passed into immortality. The nation halts; the poor line the streets for a fortnight of mourning, the flowers of Buenos Aires exhausted before the grief. Perón has lost the abanderada of his movement. Her embalmed body, meant for a great monument never built, is about to begin an odyssey stranger than any in his own long journey.
stops.quote: Eva Perón entró en la inmortalidad.
stops.quote_source: National radio announcement of Eva Perón's death, 26 July 1952

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the bombing of the Plaza
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June the navy and rebel air force turn on the capital itself: aircraft cross the sky over Buenos Aires and drop more than a hundred bombs, nine to fourteen tons of explosive, onto the Plaza de Mayo to kill the president and his cabinet. They miss Perón but slaughter the people: some three hundred dead, near a thousand wounded, most of them civilians crossing the square, a trolley of workers among the bodies. It is a massacre without precedent in the city's history, and the prelude, in three months, to his fall.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Revolución Libertadora and the fall
stops.campa: In September the self-styled Revolución Libertadora rises across the country, and by the nineteenth Perón resigns rather than plunge Argentina into civil war. Ten years to the month since the descamisados carried him to the balcony, the conductor is thrown down. He seeks asylum in the Paraguayan embassy and takes refuge aboard the Paraguayan gunboat in the river. The victors will ban his very name; to say 'Perón' becomes a crime. Thus begins an exile that will last eighteen years, and a resistance that will not die.

stops.name: Asunción and Villarrica, the first refuge
stops.campa: A Paraguayan flying-boat carries the fallen president across the border in early October, and he is sheltered first in Asunción and then, from the seventeenth, the sacred date of his movement, in the country estate of a Colorado leader at Villarrica among the orange groves. The people of Paraguay throng to glimpse him; the exile is already a legend. But Argentine pressure closes in, and in early November a plane lifts him away toward Central America. The odyssey of the exiled conductor, like San Martín's and O'Higgins's before him, is truly begun.

stops.name: Colón, Panama: the exile and the meeting with Isabel
stops.campa: In Panama the exile lives modestly: the Hotel Washington in Colón, then a small chalet lent by the town. And here, in the cabaret Happyland, he meets a dancer of twenty-four, María Estela Martínez, called Isabel, touring with a ballet company. He buys out her contract for three hundred dollars, and by late January she is his companion. As Eva rose from the radio, Isabel rises from the cabaret; the widower takes to his side the woman who will one day, incredibly, succeed him as president of Argentina.

stops.name: Caracas, exile under the Venezuelan sun
stops.campa: From Panama, by way of Nicaragua and Maracaibo, Perón reaches Caracas in August and settles in the Venezuela of Pérez Jiménez. From here he directs the first threads of the Peronist Resistance at home, where his followers strike and sabotage and scrawl his forbidden name on every wall. He nearly perishes in a bomb attack on his residence. When Pérez Jiménez is overthrown in January 1958 the ground shifts under him again, and he must move on to the last and strangest of his Caribbean stations.

stops.name: Ciudad Trujillo, the court of the dictator
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of January Perón lands in the Dominican Republic, in the capital that the tyrant Trujillo has named after himself. He lodges at the Jaragua, then, for economy, the Hotel Paz. For two years he lives under the shadow of the most absolute despot of the Caribbean, plotting his return by letter and messenger. When even this refuge sours, on the twenty-sixth of January 1960 he boards a plane once more, this time for Spain, and the villa at Puerta de Hierro where the long heart of the exile awaits.

stops.name: Madrid, the villa at Puerta de Hierro
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of January Perón reaches Franco's Spain and settles at last in a quinta near Puerta de Hierro on the edge of Madrid, the house they call 17 de Octubre. Here he will spend twelve of his eighteen exiled years and govern Argentina from afar. Pilgrims of Peronism cross the ocean to kiss his hand; he receives union bosses and young guerrillas alike, dispensing tapes, letters, and cryptic blessings to every faction. From this suburban villa, by messenger and magnetic tape, the banned old conductor rules a country that will not let him go.

stops.name: Milan, the hidden corpse of Eva
stops.campa: While Perón wanders his exile, the body of Eva undergoes an odyssey of its own. The Revolución Libertadora, fearing the dead saint more than the living leader, steals the embalmed corpse and hides it, at last burying it in secret under a false name, María Maggi de Magistris, in the Musocco cemetery of Milan. For sixteen years the incorruptible Evita lies concealed in Italian soil while the man who loved her governs from Madrid. Only in 1971 will the generals confess the grave and return her to him.

stops.name: Puerta de Hierro, Eva restored
stops.campa: On the third of September the coffin comes home to Puerta de Hierro. After sixteen years lost, the body of Eva is returned to Perón in Madrid, still uncannily preserved. In the villa it is kept, and the tale runs that José López Rega, the dark occultist counselor now shadowing the household, performs his rites over the corpse, seeking to pass Eva's power into Isabel, the third wife. The saint of the descamisados lies again beside the conductor, on the eve of his impossible return, wrapped now in rumor and in cult.

stops.name: Ezeiza, the first return, 17 November 1972
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November, after seventeen years of banishment, Perón lands at Ezeiza on Argentine soil, an old man of seventy-seven stepping off the plane into a downpour and a sea of the faithful, held back by the still-frightened generals. He stays only weeks, but the spell is broken: the exile has touched the homeland and lived. He anoints Héctor Cámpora to run in his place, and Cámpora wins. The road is open now for the definitive return, and for the tragedy that will stain it.

stops.name: Ezeiza, the return and the massacre, 20 June 1973
stops.campa: On the twentieth of June Perón returns for good, and the greatest crowd in Argentine history, some two million, floods the highways to Ezeiza to receive him. But at the speakers' platform, right-wing Peronists open fire on the leftist columns of the Montoneros and the FAR as they approach: thirteen dead, hundreds wounded, the woods of Ezeiza turned to a killing ground. The old man's plane is diverted; the day of homecoming becomes a massacre. The two faces of his movement, the union right and the guerrilla left, have drawn each other's blood at the very hour of his triumph.
